title: Israel's 11-Day Escalated Assault on Hebron
author: Monjed Jado

Palestinians stage a protest demanding to be allowed to return to their homes
on November 1, 2026 in Hebron, occupied West Bank. Photo by Mamoun
Wazwaz/Anadolu via Getty Images.

HEBRON, Occupied West Bank--Baher Sultan returned to his home in Hebron's
Khallet al-Maghariba neighborhood on Monday, nine days after Israeli soldiers
arrived at his front door and ordered his family to leave. Sultan, his wife,
and his four children were among thousands of families forcibly displaced
during a massive Israeli military operation in the city.

The house they returned to had been ransacked. Sultan said soldiers had
occupied the home for several days, rifling through cupboards, breaking
windows and door locks, and damaging household furniture and other belongings.

Despite the damage and the disruption to their lives, Sultan, 47, said his
family was overjoyed simply to be back in their neighborhood. "We returned on
the same day the army withdrew. I couldn't wait," he told Drop Site News.

The Israeli army's 11-day assault on Hebron followed an October 23 attack by
two Palestinian gunmen on a military checkpoint in the city that killed two
Israeli soldiers before the two gunmen were shot dead. Israeli Prime Minister
Benjamin Netanyahu visited the city soon afterwards and announced a major
military operation. "The IDF will enter the neighborhoods from which the
terrorists emerged, evacuate the residents, go house-to-house, and dismantle
the terror infrastructure. We are prepared for an extensive operation in Judea
and Samaria," he said, using Israel's name for the West Bank.

Sultan said the ordeal began on October 24, when Israeli soldiers raided his
neighborhood and began knocking on residents' doors.

"We had been frightened from the moment the occupation government made its
announcement. We were watching what was happening, and when the army spread
through the neighbourhood and the loudspeakers started, we became scared and
confused," he said. "Soldiers got out of their vehicles and began knocking on
doors. When I opened the door, they asked who lived there and took my identity
card. I told them, and then they informed me that I had to leave the house and
take only a few essential belongings. Some of them were shouting [in Hebrew],
and we couldn't understand what they were saying, but we were frightened."

The Israeli military sealed all the entrances to the city before moving in,
displacing nearly 5,000 Palestinians, demolishing buildings, and disrupting
schooling for some 80,000 students. Families in the Al-Jalda and Deir Bahha
neighborhoods were all ordered to flee, while residents of other neighborhoods
were subjected to a strict military cordon.

As the assault was under way, the UN agency for Palestinian refugees (UNRWA)[
warned](https://english.wafa.ps/Pages/Details/176396) on October 27 that the
Israeli military operation carried alarming echoes of the 2025 Israeli assault
on three refugee camps in the northern West Bank that displaced over 32,000
Palestinians in what Human Rights Watch found amounted to war crimes and
crimes against humanity.

The soldiers left Sultan and his family to make their way through the streets
after ordering them to flee the neighborhood. They spent the first two days
moving between relatives' homes before his cousin offered them his apartment
in the Sheikh neighbourhood, near Bab al-Zawiya in central Hebron, where they
stayed for the next five days without knowing how long their displacement
would last.

His children, out of school since the first day of the military operation,
struggled to adjust to the unfamiliar environment.

"They don't feel free to move around, and they feel shy and embarrassed
whenever they do anything, like asking for food or going to the bathroom. They
don't talk about it, so as not to embarrass our cousins," Sultan told Drop
Site while the family was still displaced. "Their needs go beyond food and
shelter. They need a space to move around, books and notebooks, and an
education that allows them to carry on with a normal life."

The Israeli army withdrew from the occupied neighborhoods at dawn on November
2, saying it had completed its operations after confiscating a grand
[total](https://www.haaretz.com/west-bank/2026-11-02/ty-article/.premium/idf-
says-it-seized-just-4-weapons-in-major-10-day-raid-in-west-banks-
hebron/000001a1-9b87-d1dd-abbd-dbdfe7c20000) of four weapons. Families began
returning to their damaged homes in Al-Jalda and Deir Bahha that same day, and
schools, universities, and businesses began to reopen, Mayor Yousef al-Jabari
told Al Jazeera.

Most homes in Khallet al-Maghariba sustained light to moderate damage, Sultan
said, with broken windows among the most visible signs of the operation,
adding that some residents believed some of the damage was caused by the
deployment of Israeli snipers in the area.

His children have also returned to school. "They are happy now," he said.

## **A City Ravaged by Occupation**

Located in the southern West Bank, Hebron is the largest city in the territory
with some 200,000 residents, and for decades has been one of the most tightly
controlled by the Israeli occupation.

Unlike other cities in the West Bank that are ringed by Israeli settlements,
usually on the surrounding hilltops, in Hebron Israeli settlements exist in
the heart of the city, with armed Israeli settlers living in the midst of
Palestinians residents. Also unlike other cities in the West Bank, Hebron did
not receive the status of Area A under the Oslo Accords.

In 1997, the Palestinian Liberation Organization and the Israeli government
signed the [Hebron Protoco](https://www.un.org/unispal/document/auto-
insert-196311/)l which split the city into two sections: H1, comprising 80% of
the city that is nominally under Palestinian control, and H2, comprising 20%
of the city that is under full Israeli military control, and includes the Old
City and the historic Ibrahimi Mosque. Some 40,000 Palestinians live in H2
alongside several hundred settlers with a heavy Israeli military presence. The
city also holds about [40
percent](https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2026/10/11/creating-a-ghost-town-
lives-in-limbo-behind-israeli-gates-and-checkpoints) of the West Bank's 89
main checkpoints and 11 percent of all 925 movement obstacles in the
territory, according to the UN.

The Hebron Protocol was signed in the wake of the 1994 Ibrahimi Mosque
massacre, when Baruch Goldstein, an American-born settler, [opened
fire](https://www.palestine-studies.org/en/node/1652605) on Palestinians
praying at the Ibrahimi Mosque, killing 29 worshippers.

Israel [responded](https://www.arabnews.com/node/298389) by partitioning the
mosque and closing Shuhada Street, the Old City's main commercial artery, to
Palestinians. By 2007, 1,829 businesses in the city center had shut, about 440
of them by military order.

"Today those who rule Israel are followers of the man who carried out the
massacre, and they are seeking to displace and expel us," Sultan said,
referring to Itamar Ben-Gvir, Israel's national security minister, who [kept a
portrait of Goldstein](https://www.ynetnews.com/article/BJJZ26hlU) on his
living room wall for years before entering government.

For Sultan, who lived through the 1994 massacre, Israel's latest operation was
almost as bad. He says that back then at least the Israeli government still
felt compelled to publicly condemn the violence, however nominally.

"Today, those committing the displacement, killing, and demolition are the
government and the right-wing extremists in it," he said.

For residents returning to their homes this week, the attack and their
subsequent displacement are part of a much longer story.

## **Mass Expulsion**

Abdul Shakour Mujahid said his was the first house in the neighborhood of Al-
Jalda that was raided by the Israeli military.

"They told me I had an hour to take my most important things, and that I was
only allowed to take simple things, clothes and some belongings," he said.

The troops also confiscated his car, and what he was able to carry on foot was
not enough for him, his wife, and their three children, the eldest of whom is
12.

Mujahid and his family moved into his father's home in an adjacent
neighborhood. In addition to relying on his father for food, he received an
aid package of basic supplies and milk from the local relief committee. From a
distance, he watched soldiers spread across the rooftops of Al-Jalda, where
they used dozens of houses as sniper positions.

"The feeling is hard to describe. It is a new Nakba for us, to see your home
before your eyes and not be able to reach it," he said, invoking the Arabic
word for "catastrophe" that Palestinians use to describe their mass expulsion
by Zionist forces in 1948. "It is the greatest crime and the greatest
injustice. We have done nothing. What helps us endure is the embrace of family
and relatives in the community."

The Hebron Governorate Support and Relief Committee registered 537 affected
families, comprising 3,361 people, including 232 infants, 1,193 children aged
between two and 17, 326 elderly people, 147 pregnant or breastfeeding women,
32 people with disabilities, and 213 people with chronic illnesses, according
to its head Sufian Al-Muhtaseb.

"Hebron's communities refused to open shelters and declared they were ready to
host displaced families [in their homes], and the invitations were not limited
to relatives," Al-Muhtaseb told Drop Site

Al-Muhtaseb said there were severe supply shortages, with the hardest requests
the committee received being food and drink--and, above all, baby formula.

"The occupation did not allow residents to take their money from their homes,
and they find it hard to ask the families they are staying with, even if they
are relatives, and even those they went to may not be in a good financial
situation," he said.

## **A Ripple Effect**

On October 29, Adalah, a legal center for Palestinian citizens of Israel,[
petitioned](http://www.jpost.com/israel-news/defense-news/article-913537)
Israel's High Court on behalf of the municipality and seven residents of Al-
Jalda and Ein Deir Bahha.

The petition said troops forced hundreds of families from their homes late at
night with little notice, barred their return indefinitely, and provided no
concrete justification for an evacuation on that scale, which it argued
amounted to forcible transfer and collective punishment under the Fourth
Geneva Convention.

It also cited municipal figures showing that the closure had left about 1,200
tonnes of rubbish piling up in the city, as garbage trucks could not reach the
sealed areas.

Hebron Mayor Yousef al-Jabari told Drop Site the municipality worked with
partner organizations to provide aid to affected families.

"The municipality is preparing a survey to identify residents' needs and
priorities so that aid can be directed according to each family's actual
circumstances," al-Jabari said before the Israeli withdrawal.

During the operation, Israeli forces demolished 15 homes and other structures
and forced 327 shops to close, exacting a severe toll on the city's economy--
one of the most important in the West Bank.

The city [accounts](https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2026/10/25/why-israels-
latest-assault-on-hebron-is-so-significant-for-the-west-bank) for about 40% of
Palestinian industrial output in the West Bank and 30% of exports, and the
closure of whole areas and restrictions on the movement of workers and goods
halted factories, markets, and supply chains, while businesses and shops
struggled to keep operating.

Adnan al-Natsheh, deputy head of the Hebron Chamber of Commerce and Industry,
said the direct losses from the closures "amount to between 10 million and 12
million shekels a day," or about $3.2 million to $3.8 million, including about
1 million shekels in the dairy sector alone.

He warned that hundreds of industrial and commercial businesses have been
affected, and said 13 facilities in the Farsh al-Hawa area had suffered
vandalism, bulldozing, and demolition.

"The restrictions on workers and goods threaten entire production and supply
chains across the West Bank."
